subject: history
title: Rivers, cities, and the first states
objective: Connect settlement, surplus, specialized work, records, and authority while separating evidence from inference.

lesson.opening: Early cities grew through connected changes rather than one automatic chain. Environmental conditions shaped choices, while institutions and people organized work in different ways.

sections.heading: Start with the setting
sections.body: Rivers could support farming and transport, but they also brought floods, drought, and disputes over water. A historical explanation should name the environmental feature before claiming what it caused.

sections.heading: Trace a possible sequence
sections.body: A surplus of food could support coordinated labor and specialized work. Record keeping might then help institutions track goods and obligations. This is a model to test, not a universal rule.

sections.heading: Separate evidence from inference
sections.body: A storehouse, tablet, or settlement layer is evidence. The claim that it proves a particular political arrangement is an inference. Good history marks that boundary and asks what other evidence would support it.

sections.heading: Compare sources carefully
sections.body: A building record and a later narrative may describe the same society for different purposes. Compare what each source preserves, what it leaves out, and who had reason to create it.

activities.prompt: Compare one advantage and one constraint of the Nile and Tigris–Euphrates settings.
activities.instructions: Use a concrete environmental feature and explain how it could affect organized work.

activities.prompt: Arrange this account from material condition to political consequence.
activities.instructions: Treat this as a reasoned model, not a claim that every city followed one automatic path.

activities.prompt: Which link in your account is an inference rather than a directly observed fact, and what evidence could test it?
activities.instructions: Name the inference and propose one kind of surviving evidence.

activities.prompt: Compare a material record, such as a tablet or building, with a later written account of the same society.
activities.instructions: Explain one strength and one limitation of each source before drawing a conclusion.
